gpt-b1-first-professional-result.q: You ask ChatGPT to "write me a product description" and get a generic, forgettable paragraph you can't use. Per the lesson's prompt formula, what's the single biggest fix?
options: Ask ChatGPT to write it twice and pick the better one
Switch to a longer, more expensive model
Add role, audience, context, explicit requirements, and format to the prompt
Tell ChatGPT to 'try harder' and be more creative
gpt-b1-first-professional-result.why: Each part of the prompt (role, context, requirements, format) removes a guess ChatGPT would otherwise make, which is why a vague one-liner produces generic output.

gpt-b1-first-professional-result.q: Why does adding a line like 'Do not use the words stunning or must-see' improve a ChatGPT draft?
options: It closes off the laziest, most generic wrong answers before they happen
It shortens the response automatically
It's a required OpenAI content-policy field
It guarantees factual accuracy in the draft
gpt-b1-first-professional-result.why: The 'do not' line rules out the cliché, low-effort phrasing ChatGPT tends to default to, forcing a more specific result.

gpt-b1-first-professional-result.q: A freelancer writes a detailed, well-structured prompt, gets a draft back, and sends it straight to the client without comparing it to their original requirements. What mistake does this match from the lesson?
options: Forgetting to state the audience
Not specifying format or length
Typing a vague one-line request
Accepting the first draft without checking it actually hit the specific requirements listed
gpt-b1-first-professional-result.why: Even a well-structured prompt can produce a draft that misses a requirement; the lesson stresses checking the result against your original need before using it.

gpt-b2-prompt-structure-fundamentals.q: A ChatGPT response comes back rambling, three times longer than needed, with no clear structure. Which part of the 4-part formula was most likely missing or vague?
options: Role
Format
Context
Constraints
gpt-b2-prompt-structure-fundamentals.why: The lesson states a rambling, wrong-length answer usually traces back to a missing or vague Format instruction.

gpt-b2-prompt-structure-fundamentals.q: ChatGPT gives a confident, well-written answer — to a problem you didn't actually ask about. What's the most likely cause?
options: The Format line was too short
Custom Instructions weren't set
The Task line crammed two unrelated tasks into one sentence
The model needs a system prompt
gpt-b2-prompt-structure-fundamentals.why: An answer that solves the wrong problem usually means the Task line tried to do two things at once instead of stating one specific action.

gpt-b2-prompt-structure-fundamentals.q: A prompt's result falls short. What does the lesson recommend as the most efficient next step?
options: Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch every time
Switch tools immediately
Add more adjectives describing the desired tone
Diagnose which single part (role, context, task, or format) was missing or vague, and fix only that
gpt-b2-prompt-structure-fundamentals.why: Learning to diagnose which of the four parts is missing is more useful than any single prompt template, and it avoids unnecessary full rewrites.

gpt-b3-improving-drafts-and-tone.q: You want a ChatGPT draft to sound like you, not like a generic AI. What's the most reliable technique from the lesson?
options: Paste 2-3 sentences of your own writing as a voice anchor for it to match
Repeat 'make it more professional' until it sounds right
Regenerate the response from scratch several times
Ask it to shorten the draft by half
gpt-b3-improving-drafts-and-tone.why: A real voice sample gives ChatGPT a concrete target to match, which works far better than describing style in adjectives.

gpt-b3-improving-drafts-and-tone.q: Why does 'more direct, less corporate' work better as a revision request than 'make it better'?
options: It uses simpler vocabulary the model parses faster
It gives ChatGPT a concrete, comparative target instead of an abstract adjective to guess at
It automatically shortens the response
It's the only phrasing ChatGPT recognizes as a tone request
gpt-b3-improving-drafts-and-tone.why: Generic tone requests give no fixed target and get guessed at generically; direct comparative language converges in fewer rounds.

gpt-b3-improving-drafts-and-tone.q: While revising a draft, you ask ChatGPT to fix the tone, cut the length, and restructure it all in the same follow-up. What problem does the lesson warn this causes?
options: ChatGPT will refuse the request
It uses more of your monthly quota
It becomes hard to tell which change actually fixed (or broke) the draft
It forces a full account upgrade
gpt-b3-improving-drafts-and-tone.why: Asking for tone, length, and structure to all change at once is a listed common mistake because it obscures what worked.

gpt-i1-analyzing-files-and-documents.q: You upload a 22-page contract and ask 'what's the termination clause?' without telling ChatGPT to answer only from the file. What's the risk?
options: ChatGPT will refuse to read the PDF
The file will be permanently stored without consent
ChatGPT will always cite the wrong page number
ChatGPT may blend general knowledge about contracts with the actual document, and you won't be able to tell which is which
gpt-i1-analyzing-files-and-documents.why: Without the 'only from the attached file' guardrail, ChatGPT tends to blend outside knowledge with document content indistinguishably.

gpt-i1-analyzing-files-and-documents.q: Why does the lesson insist on requiring a page or section citation for every claim ChatGPT pulls from a document?
options: It turns each answer into something you can verify in seconds instead of trusting blindly
It's a formatting requirement of the PDF standard
It prevents the file from exceeding size limits
It automatically fixes OCR errors in scanned documents
gpt-i1-analyzing-files-and-documents.why: Citations let you flip to the source and confirm a claim in seconds rather than accepting it on faith.

gpt-i1-analyzing-files-and-documents.q: You upload a scanned image-only PDF with no extractable text and ask for exact figures. What should you expect?
options: Perfect detail recall, since ChatGPT reads all PDFs identically
Reduced accuracy — a scanned image with no extractable text won't give reliable detail recall
An automatic upgrade to OCR mode
A rejection of the file with no analysis attempted
gpt-i1-analyzing-files-and-documents.why: The lesson lists uploading a scanned image with no extractable text and expecting perfect recall as a common mistake.

gpt-i2-projects-for-organized-work.q: A consultant juggles five active clients in ChatGPT. Per the lesson, what's the best way to organize this in Projects?
options: One giant Project called 'All Clients' holding every file and chat
One Project per active client, each with its own instructions and files
No Projects — just rely on memory to keep clients straight
A new Project for every single chat message
gpt-i2-projects-for-organized-work.why: A Project is meant to be one workspace per active engagement, not one giant catch-all archive.

gpt-i2-projects-for-organized-work.q: Why do Project instructions save time compared to a normal chat?
options: They unlock a cheaper pricing tier
They replace the need to write any prompt at all
They apply automatically to every chat inside that Project, instead of being restated each time
They sync identically across every other Project you own
gpt-i2-projects-for-organized-work.why: Project instructions are written once and apply to every chat inside that Project, so a new chat already starts grounded.

gpt-i2-projects-for-organized-work.q: A Project starts giving answers based on an old version of a client's brief. What's the likely mistake?
options: The Project was named after a specific client instead of a category
Project instructions were written at all
Too many files were uploaded
The source documents were updated, but the files in the Project were never re-uploaded
gpt-i2-projects-for-organized-work.why: Forgetting to re-upload files when underlying documents change means the Project answers from a stale version.

gpt-i3-custom-gpts-for-repeatable-tasks.q: A custom GPT gives inconsistent, drifting answers depending on how a teammate phrases their request. What's the most likely design flaw?
options: Too few knowledge files were uploaded
The GPT's purpose is too broad or multi-task, so its behavior drifts
Web search wasn't enabled
It was tested with an edge case before launch
gpt-i3-custom-gpts-for-repeatable-tasks.why: Custom GPTs fail most often from trying to do too much; naming one job is what keeps behavior consistent.

gpt-i3-custom-gpts-for-repeatable-tasks.q: Why does the lesson recommend testing a custom GPT with a deliberately weird or off-topic input before sharing it with a team?
options: It's required to publish a GPT
It increases the GPT's visibility in Explore GPTs
That's exactly where vague instructions break down, and it's cheap to catch early
It unlocks the code interpreter tool automatically
gpt-i3-custom-gpts-for-repeatable-tasks.why: Off-topic or edge-case inputs are where a poorly scoped GPT's instructions break down, and catching that before a teammate does is cheap.

gpt-i3-custom-gpts-for-repeatable-tasks.q: What should a custom GPT's system instructions define for requests outside its one job?
options: A specific boundary response so it declines instead of improvising
Nothing — it should always attempt to help regardless of scope
A redirect to Deep Research
An automatic tone shift to match the off-topic request
gpt-i3-custom-gpts-for-repeatable-tasks.why: Not setting a boundary response for out-of-scope requests leaves the GPT improvising instead of declining, which the lesson flags as a common mistake.

gpt-i4-deep-research-reports.q: You get roughly 10 Deep Research runs a month on Plus. What should you do before spending one on a real question?
options: Submit the first version of the question that comes to mind
Run the same question twice to compare results
Draft and refine the research brief in a normal chat first, then paste the tightened version into Deep Research
Skip scoping — Deep Research automatically narrows vague questions
gpt-i4-deep-research-reports.why: Iterating on the brief in a free regular chat first avoids burning a limited monthly run on a question that still needed shaping.

gpt-i4-deep-research-reports.q: Why does the lesson stress naming which source types to include or exclude in a Deep Research brief?
options: It's a mandatory field in the composer
It limits the report to under 500 words
It disables citation requirements
Without it, the report can end up unfocused, mixing outdated or low-credibility sources with current, reliable ones
gpt-i4-deep-research-reports.why: Not scoping source types is a listed common mistake that produces an unfocused report mixing outdated and current information.

gpt-i4-deep-research-reports.q: A Deep Research report just finished. What should you do before treating any specific claim in it as fact?
options: Immediately forward it to your team as final
Read the source list and check a sample of citations against the underlying sources
Re-run the exact same query to confirm it
Delete the original brief so it doesn't bias future runs
gpt-i4-deep-research-reports.why: Treating the report as final truth without checking citations is a named common mistake; spot-checking sources first is the guardrail.

gpt-a1-data-analysis-with-code-interpret.q: ChatGPT returns a confident month-over-month growth analysis on a CSV, but it turns out 3 duplicate rows inflated the numbers. What step in the lesson's workflow was skipped?
options: Requesting a labeled chart
The data-quality check step (columns, row count, missing values, duplicates) before running the analysis
Uploading the file as XLSX instead of CSV
Verifying at least one number by hand
gpt-a1-data-analysis-with-code-interpret.why: Skipping the data-quality check is the most common failure mode, producing confidently wrong analysis on dirty data.

gpt-a1-data-analysis-with-code-interpret.q: Why does the lesson insist on asking ChatGPT to 'show the calculation logic, not just the result'?
options: It turns the analysis into something you can audit in seconds instead of a black box you either trust blindly or don't use
It's required for chart generation to work
It automatically catches every hallucination
It makes the Python code run faster
gpt-a1-data-analysis-with-code-interpret.why: Visible calculation logic is what lets you audit the analysis quickly instead of trusting it blindly.

gpt-a1-data-analysis-with-code-interpret.q: A computed number in a spreadsheet analysis looks off. What's the fastest way to find the bug, per the lesson?
options: Re-upload the file and start over from scratch
Switch to a different ChatGPT plan
Ignore it — code interpreter results are always accurate
Ask 'show me the code you ran' and read it to spot the wrong column, filter, or date range
gpt-a1-data-analysis-with-code-interpret.why: The proTip explicitly recommends reading the underlying code to spot the bug faster than re-explaining the task.

gpt-a2-memory-and-personalization.q: You need to discuss a confidential client detail you don't want ChatGPT to remember or keep in your history. What should you do?
options: Add it as an explicit memory, then delete it right after
Ask ChatGPT to promise not to remember it
Start a Temporary Chat, which never touches memory or history
Use a Project instead of a regular chat
gpt-a2-memory-and-personalization.why: Temporary Chat is the lesson's safe default for confidential or one-off content because it never touches memory or history.

gpt-a2-memory-and-personalization.q: What's the actual difference between Custom Instructions and memory, per the lesson?
options: They are two names for the exact same feature
Custom Instructions are standing rules you set explicitly; memory accumulates from conversation unless you actively curate it
Memory only works inside Projects
Custom Instructions require an Enterprise plan
gpt-a2-memory-and-personalization.why: The lesson explicitly distinguishes explicit standing rules (Custom Instructions) from passively accumulating, curatable memory.

gpt-a2-memory-and-personalization.q: Several months into using ChatGPT, responses start referencing an old job you no longer have. What mistake led to this?
options: Never reviewing and cleaning up memory, letting outdated facts quietly skew responses
Doing a quarterly memory review
Using Temporary Chat for sensitive topics
Adding a deliberate memory about a standing preference
gpt-a2-memory-and-personalization.why: Never reviewing memory is a listed common mistake that lets outdated facts silently skew future responses.

gpt-a3-agent-mode-and-your-workflow.q: You give Agent mode the instruction 'help me plan an event' with no finish condition or output format. What typically happens?
options: It completes the task in one step automatically
It asks you a single clarifying question and stops
It keeps browsing and acting without ever producing a usable, finished result
It defaults to writing a Deep Research report instead
gpt-a3-agent-mode-and-your-workflow.why: A vague goal with no finish condition is a named common mistake that leaves Agent mode wandering without a usable result.

gpt-a3-agent-mode-and-your-workflow.q: The lesson has you explicitly tell Agent mode to 'stop and ask before submitting any form, logging in, or making a payment,' even though Agent mode already pauses for these by default. Why state it anyway?
options: It's a legal requirement for using Agent mode
It speeds up how fast the agent completes tasks
It disables the terminal access entirely
It makes an already-default safety boundary explicit and unambiguous in your specific task
gpt-a3-agent-mode-and-your-workflow.why: Stating the pause instruction directly makes an already-default guardrail unambiguous for this specific task.

gpt-a3-agent-mode-and-your-workflow.q: Agent mode successfully completes a multi-step venue-booking task you know you'll need to repeat monthly. What's the recommended next move?
options: Convert the reusable subtask into a custom GPT or Project instruction so it's not re-described from scratch every time
Delete the chat so it doesn't clutter your history
Re-run the exact same Agent mode task every month from a blank chat
Switch future runs to Deep Research instead
gpt-a3-agent-mode-and-your-workflow.why: The lesson explicitly warns against running a good task once and never converting it into a repeatable custom GPT or Project setup.
